claim: The deer mouse (genus Peromyscus) is the most abundant mammal in North America.
source: The deer mouse (genus Peromyscus) is the most abundant mammal in North America, and it occupies almost every type of terrestrial habitat.
evidence: This is a direct factual statement in the abstract, drawing from established knowledge about Peromyscus abundance.

claim: Peromyscus occupies almost every type of terrestrial habitat in North America.
source: The deer mouse (genus Peromyscus) is the most abundant mammal in North America, and it occupies almost every type of terrestrial habitat.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the extensive distribution data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The deer mouse has contributed to understanding of population genetics, disease ecology, longevity, endocrinology and behavior for decades.
source: For decades, the deer mouse has contributed to our understanding of population genetics, disease ecology, longevity, endocrinology and behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by the extensive literature review and citations throughout the manuscript documenting research in these areas.

claim: The first Peromyscus specimens were shipped to European systematicists in the late 18th century.
source: When the first Peromyscus specimens were shipped to European systematicists in the late 18th century, their resemblance to the local wood mouse prompted the designation Mus sylvaticus (Hooper, 1968).
evidence: This historical claim is supported by a citation to Hooper, 1968.

claim: Early Peromyscus specimens resembled the European wood mouse, prompting the designation Mus sylvaticus.
source: When the first Peromyscus specimens were shipped to European systematicists in the late 18th century, their resemblance to the local wood mouse prompted the designation Mus sylvaticus (Hooper, 1968).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Hooper, 1968.

claim: Most rodents were assigned the generic term Mus by Linnaeus in 1758.
source: At the time, little was known of the diversity of rodents worldwide and most were assigned the generic term Mus (Linnaeus, 1758).
evidence: This is a historical taxonomic fact supported by citation to Linnaeus, 1758.

claim: The name Peromyscus was first employed by Gloger in 1841.
source: The name Peromyscus (Gloger, 1841) was first employed, albeit narrowly, in the middle of the 19th century.
evidence: This is a historical taxonomic fact supported by citation to Gloger, 1841.

claim: Quadrupeds of North America recognized only three species now known to belong to Peromyscus.
source: Quadrupeds of North America (Audubon and Bachman, 1854) recognized only three species now known to belong to Peromyscus, and Mammals of North America (Baird, 1859) included a mere 12.
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citations to Audubon and Bachman, 1854.

claim: Mammals of North America included 12 Peromyscus species in 1859.
source: Quadrupeds of North America (Audubon and Bachman, 1854) recognized only three species now known to belong to Peromyscus, and Mammals of North America (Baird, 1859) included a mere 12.
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citation to Baird, 1859.

claim: By the turn of the 20th century, Peromyscus included 143 forms, 42 of which represented monotypic or good biological species.
source: But by the turn of the 20th century, Peromyscus included 143 forms, 42 of which represented monotypic or good biological species (Osgood, 1909).
evidence: This historical taxonomic claim is supported by citation to Osgood, 1909.

claim: Today 56 species of Peromyscus are recognized.
source: Today 56 species are recognized, the most widespread and diverse being Peromyscus maniculatus (Musser and Carleton, 2005).
evidence: This current taxonomic fact is supported by citation to Musser and Carleton, 2005.

claim: Peromyscus maniculatus is the most widespread and diverse species of Peromyscus.
source: Today 56 species are recognized, the most widespread and diverse being Peromyscus maniculatus (Musser and Carleton, 2005).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation to Musser and Carleton, 2005.

claim: Peromyscus includes more species than any other North American mammalian genus.
source: Thus, although not immediately appreciated, Peromyscus includes more species than any other North American mammalian genus and, apart from Mus and Rattus, more is known concerning its biology in the laboratory than any other group of small mammals (Figure 1; King, 1968; Kirkland and Layne, 1989).
evidence: This comparative claim is supported by citations to King, 1968 and Kirkland and Layne, 1989.

claim: Apart from Mus and Rattus, more is known concerning Peromyscus biology in the laboratory than any other group of small mammals.
source: Thus, although not immediately appreciated, Peromyscus includes more species than any other North American mammalian genus and, apart from Mus and Rattus, more is known concerning its biology in the laboratory than any other group of small mammals (Figure 1; King, 1968; Kirkland and Layne, 1989).
evidence: This comparative claim is supported by citations to King, 1968 and Kirkland and Layne, 1989.

claim: Peromyscus has been labeled as 'the Drosophila of North American mammalogy'.
source: Several disciplines including ecology, evolution, physiology, reproductive biology and behavioral neuroscience have all employed Peromyscus, inspiring its label as 'the Drosophila of North American mammalogy' (Dewey and Dawson, 2001).
evidence: This characterization is supported by citation to Dewey and Dawson, 2001.

claim: Peromyscus belong to the Cricetidae family.
source: Peromyscus belong to the Cricetidae family, which includes voles (Microtus), hamsters (Mesocricetus), and New World rats and mice.
evidence: This taxonomic relationship is stated in the Figure 1 caption and shown in the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Muridae and Cricetidae diverged roughly 25 million years ago.
source: Muridae and Cricetidae diverged roughly 25 million years ago. Schematic based on based on phylogeny data from Steppan et al. (2004).
evidence: This evolutionary timing is stated in Figure 1 caption and supported by citation to Steppan et al., 2004.

claim: Members of the genus Peromyscus are distributed from the southern edge of the Canadian Arctic to the Colombian border of Panama.
source: Members of the genus are distributed from the southern edge of the Canadian Arctic to the Colombian border of Panama (Figure 2).
evidence: This geographic distribution is stated directly and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Demographic and biogeographic factors have influenced the diversity and distribution of deer mice.
source: Various demographic and biogeographic factors (e.g., Pleistocene glacial and pluvial cycles, population expansions, mountain range elevations and sea-level changes) have influenced the diversity and distribution of deer mice (Sullivan et al., 1997; Riddle et al., 2000; Dragoo et al., 2006; Kalkvik et al., 2012; López-González et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting these biogeographic influences.

claim: Osgood's 1909 taxonomic revision was built on examinations of more than 27,000 specimens.
source: Osgood's influential 1909 taxonomic revision was built on examinations of more than 27,000 specimens from diverse locales that were collected primarily by the US Biological Survey.
evidence: This historical fact about the scope of Osgood's work is stated directly.

claim: More than 120,000 Peromyscus specimens are accessioned in Natural History museums across North America and the United Kingdom.
source: Today, more than 120,000 Peromyscus specimens are accessioned in Natural History museums across North America and the United Kingdom (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Shifts in the distributions of deer mice have been linked to climate change by comparing past and present-day collecting locales.
source: For example, by comparing past and present-day collecting locales, shifts in the distributions of deer mice have been linked to climate change (Moritz et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011; Rowe et al., 2014), and morphological analyses of these museum specimens reveal how deer mice respond to changing environments (Grieco and Rizk, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting climate-related distribution shifts.

claim: Morphological analyses of museum specimens reveal how deer mice respond to changing environments.
source: For example, by comparing past and present-day collecting locales, shifts in the distributions of deer mice have been linked to climate change (Moritz et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011; Rowe et al., 2014), and morphological analyses of these museum specimens reveal how deer mice respond to changing environments (Grieco and Rizk, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grieco and Rizk, 2010.

claim: Deer mice, particularly in New England, do enter human households.
source: Although not strictly commensal, deer mice (particularly in New England) do enter human households and partake of their larders.
evidence: This behavioral observation is stated directly.

claim: Walt Disney drew inspiration for Mickey Mouse from tame field mice (most likely Peromyscus leucopus) that would wander into his old Kansas City animation studio.
source: According to legend, Walt Disney drew inspiration for Mickey Mouse from the 'tame field mice' (most likely Peromyscus leucopus) that would wander into his old Kansas City animation studio (Updike, 1991).
evidence: This anecdotal claim is supported by citation to Updike, 1991.

claim: Peromyscus are most commonly trapped in woodlands and brushlands.
source: Nevertheless, Peromyscus are most commonly trapped in woodlands and brushlands and are also found in tropical and temperate rainforests, grasslands, savannas, swamps, deserts and alpine habitats (Figure 3; Baker, 1968).
evidence: This habitat preference is stated directly and supported by citation to Baker, 1968.

claim: Peromyscus are found in tropical and temperate rainforests, grasslands, savannas, swamps, deserts and alpine habitats.
source: Nevertheless, Peromyscus are most commonly trapped in woodlands and brushlands and are also found in tropical and temperate rainforests, grasslands, savannas, swamps, deserts and alpine habitats (Figure 3; Baker, 1968).
evidence: This habitat diversity is stated directly, supported by citation to Baker, 1968, and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The elevational range of P. m. sonoriensis stretches from below sea level in Death Valley to above 4300 meters in the adjacent White and Sierra Nevada mountain ranges.
source: The remarkable elevational range of one subspecies (P. m. sonoriensis) stretches from below sea level in Death Valley to above 4300 meters in the adjacent White and Sierra Nevada mountain ranges (Hock, 1964).
evidence: This specific elevational range is stated and supported by citation to Hock, 1964.

claim: The ability of deer mice to colonize and thrive in low-oxygen environments is due, in part, to standing genetic variation in globin genes.
source: The ability of deer mice to colonize and thrive in low-oxygen environments is due, in part, to standing genetic variation in globin genes (Snyder, 1981; Natarajan et al., 2015).
evidence: This mechanistic claim is supported by citations to Snyder, 1981 and Natarajan et al., 2015.

claim: Several amino acid substitutions in hemoglobin confer high hemoglobin-O2 affinity and better aerobic performance at high altitudes.
source: Storz and colleagues (2007, 2009) pinpointed several amino acid substitutions that confer high hemoglobin-O2 affinity and better aerobic performance at high altitudes.
evidence: This molecular finding is supported by citations to Storz and colleagues' work from 2007 and 2009.

claim: Functional analyses have identified how precise mutations, and interactions among mutations, affect hemoglobin-O2 affinity.
source: Functional analyses have since identified how precise mutations, and interactions among mutations, affect hemoglobin-O2 affinity, demonstrating that the adaptive value of a given biochemical substitution depends both on the local environment and the genetic background in which it arises (Natarajan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim about functional analyses is supported by citation to Natarajan et al., 2013.

claim: The adaptive value of a given biochemical substitution depends both on the local environment and the genetic background in which it arises.
source: Functional analyses have since identified how precise mutations, and interactions among mutations, affect hemoglobin-O2 affinity, demonstrating that the adaptive value of a given biochemical substitution depends both on the local environment and the genetic background in which it arises (Natarajan et al., 2013).
evidence: This general principle is stated and supported by citation to Natarajan et al., 2013.

claim: The process of adapting to urban environments leaves its mark on the genome.
source: The process of adapting to urban environments also leaves its mark on the genome (Pergams and Lacy, 2008; Munshi-South and Kharchenko, 2010; Munshi-South and Nagy, 2014).
evidence: This claim about genomic signatures of urban adaptation is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several genes associated with metabolism and immune function exhibit signatures of selection in New York City's parklands in P. leucopus.
source: By comparing the brain, liver and gonad transcriptomes of urban and rural populations of P. leucopus, Harris et al. (2013) identified several genes associated with metabolism and immune function exhibiting signatures of selection in New York City's parklands.
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2013.

claim: Renal transcripts related to solute and water balance experience purifying selection in the desert-adapted species, Peromyscus eremicus.
source: Similarly, MacManes and Eisen (2014) identified renal transcripts related to solute and water balance experiencing purifying selection in the desert-adapted species, Peromyscus eremicus.
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to MacManes and Eisen, 2014.

claim: Generally deer mice are granivores, feeding primarily on seeds.
source: Generally deer mice are granivores, feeding primarily on seeds, but fruits, fungi, green vegetation and insects have been found among their stomach contents and in the nest cavities of their burrows (Gentry and Smith, 1968; Wolff, 1985).
evidence: This dietary characterization is supported by citations to Gentry and Smith, 1968 and Wolff, 1985.

claim: Fruits, fungi, green vegetation and insects have been found among deer mouse stomach contents and in the nest cavities of their burrows.
source: Generally deer mice are granivores, feeding primarily on seeds, but fruits, fungi, green vegetation and insects have been found among their stomach contents and in the nest cavities of their burrows (Gentry and Smith, 1968; Wolff, 1985).
evidence: This dietary observation is supported by citations to Gentry and Smith, 1968 and Wolff, 1985.

claim: In the winter, Peromyscus melanotis prey almost exclusively on monarch butterflies that roost in Mexico's central highlands.
source: However, some species have evolved seasonally specialized diets. In the winter, Peromyscus melanotis prey almost exclusively on monarch butterflies that roost in Mexico's central highlands (Brower et al., 1985).
evidence: This specialized dietary behavior is supported by citation to Brower et al., 1985.

claim: On a remote island in British Columbia, Peromyscus keeni feast on auklet eggs during the seabird breeding season.
source: Moreover, on a remote island in British Columbia, Peromyscus keeni feast on auklet eggs during the seabird breeding season (Drever et al., 2000).
evidence: This specialized dietary behavior is supported by citation to Drever et al., 2000.

claim: Deer mice are common prey, contributing to the diets of many predators such as weasels, skunks, lynx, bobcats, foxes, coyotes, hawks and owls.
source: Deer mice are themselves common prey, contributing to the diets of many predators such as weasels, skunks, lynx, bobcats, foxes, coyotes, hawks and owls (Luttich et al., 1970; Bowen, 1981; Montgomery, 1989; Van Zant and Wooten, 2003).
evidence: This ecological role is supported by multiple citations documenting predation.

claim: Avian predation imposes strong selective pressure for cryptic coloration in Peromyscus.
source: Indeed, avian predation imposes strong selective pressure for cryptic coloration in Peromyscus—a classic example of local adaptation (Vignieri et al., 2010; Linnen et al., 2013).
evidence: This selective pressure is supported by citations to Vignieri et al., 2010 and Linnen et al., 2013.

claim: Common internal parasites of Peromyscus include pentastomid larvae, cestode tapeworms, nematodes and trematodes.
source: Common internal parasites include pentastomid larvae, cestode tapeworms, nematodes and trematodes (Whitaker, 1968; Pedersen and Antonovics, 2013).
evidence: This parasitological information is supported by citations to Whitaker, 1968 and Pedersen and Antonovics, 2013.

claim: External parasites of Peromyscus include lice, mites, fleas and ticks.
source: External parasites include lice, mites, fleas and ticks (Whitaker, 1968), the latter two being vectors of plague and Lyme disease, respectively (Allred, 1952; Burgdorfer et al., 1982; Gage and Kosoy, 2005).
evidence: This parasitological information is supported by citation to Whitaker, 1968.

claim: Fleas are vectors of plague.
source: External parasites include lice, mites, fleas and ticks (Whitaker, 1968), the latter two being vectors of plague and Lyme disease, respectively (Allred, 1952; Burgdorfer et al., 1982; Gage and Kosoy, 2005).
evidence: This disease vector relationship is supported by citations to Allred, 1952 and Gage and Kosoy, 2005.

claim: Ticks are vectors of Lyme disease.
source: External parasites include lice, mites, fleas and ticks (Whitaker, 1968), the latter two being vectors of plague and Lyme disease, respectively (Allred, 1952; Burgdorfer et al., 1982; Gage and Kosoy, 2005).
evidence: This disease vector relationship is supported by citations to Burgdorfer et al., 1982 and Gage and Kosoy, 2005.

claim: Peromyscus is a natural reservoir for Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterial agent of Lyme disease.
source: As a natural reservoir for Borrelia burgdorferi—the bacterial agent of Lyme disease—Peromyscus is the subject of much research on the pathogenesis and transmission of the disease (Bunikis et al., 2004; Ramamoorthi et al., 2005; Schwanz et al., 2011; Baum et al., 2012).
evidence: This disease reservoir role is supported by multiple citations.

claim: One hypothesis for the recent expansion of Lyme disease is that habitat fragmentation associated with human development favors deer mouse populations at the expense of other tick hosts that are poor reservoirs for the disease.
source: One hypothesis for the alarming recent expansion of Lyme disease is that habitat fragmentation associated with human development favors deer mouse populations at the expense of other tick hosts (e.g., squirrels and shrews) that are poor reservoirs for the disease (LoGiudice et al., 2003; Schwanz et al., 2011).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to LoGiudice et al., 2003 and Schwanz et al., 2011.

claim: Peromyscus is a carrier of the Sin Nombre hantavirus.
source: Peromyscus is also a notorious carrier of the Sin Nombre hantavirus, responsible for the deaths of 12 people in the Four Corners area of the southwestern United States in 1993.
evidence: This disease carrier role is stated directly with specific historical context.

claim: The Sin Nombre hantavirus was responsible for the deaths of 12 people in the Four Corners area of the southwestern United States in 1993.
source: Peromyscus is also a notorious carrier of the Sin Nombre hantavirus, responsible for the deaths of 12 people in the Four Corners area of the southwestern United States in 1993.
evidence: This specific historical event is stated directly.

claim: Most Peromyscus are thought to live less than a year in the wild.
source: Mortality in natural populations is incredibly high and driven by a combination of factors including limited food supply, competition for territories and predation (Bendell, 1959). As such, most Peromyscus are thought to live less than a year in the wild (Terman, 1968).
evidence: This lifespan estimate is supported by citation to Terman, 1968.

claim: Early investigators noted substantially longer natural lifespans in their laboratory colonies compared to wild populations.
source: However, early investigators noted substantially longer natural lifespans in their laboratory colonies (Sumner, 1922; Dice, 1933).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to Sumner, 1922 and Dice, 1933.

claim: P. leucopus and Mus musculus have a twofold difference in life expectancy.
source: With a twofold difference in life expectancy, Sacher and Hart (1978) proposed P. leucopus and Mus musculus as a longevity contrast pair.
evidence: This comparative longevity observation is supported by citation to Sacher and Hart, 1978.

claim: P. leucopus lives up to 8 years and may remain fertile for 5 years.
source: P. leucopus—which lives up to 8 years and may remain fertile for 5—produces fewer reactive oxygen species, exhibits enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity and less oxidative damage to lipids relative to the short-lived (~3.5 years) laboratory mouse (Sohal et al., 1993; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This lifespan and fertility information is stated directly.

claim: P. leucopus produces fewer reactive oxygen species, exhibits enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity and less oxidative damage to lipids relative to the laboratory mouse.
source: P. leucopus—which lives up to 8 years and may remain fertile for 5—produces fewer reactive oxygen species, exhibits enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity and less oxidative damage to lipids relative to the short-lived (~3.5 years) laboratory mouse (Sohal et al., 1993; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: These biochemical differences are supported by citations to Sohal et al., 1993 and Shi et al., 2013.

claim: The laboratory mouse lives approximately 3.5 years.
source: P. leucopus—which lives up to 8 years and may remain fertile for 5—produces fewer reactive oxygen species, exhibits enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity and less oxidative damage to lipids relative to the short-lived (~3.5 years) laboratory mouse (Sohal et al., 1993; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This lifespan estimate for Mus musculus is stated directly.

claim: Studies contrasting the reproductive and developmental patterns of wild and domesticated deer mice have found few significant differences.
source: Yet studies contrasting the reproductive and developmental patterns of wild and domesticated deer mice have found few significant differences (Millar, 1989; Botten et al., 2000).
evidence: This comparative finding is supported by citations to Millar, 1989 and Botten et al., 2000.

claim: Gestation in P. maniculatus ranges from 21 to 27 days with an average of 23.6 days.
source: Gestation ranges from 21 to 27 days (average 23.6) and average litter size is 4.6 pups (Millar, 1989).
evidence: This life history data is supported by citation to Millar, 1989.

claim: Average litter size in P. maniculatus is 4.6 pups.
source: Gestation ranges from 21 to 27 days (average 23.6) and average litter size is 4.6 pups (Millar, 1989).
evidence: This life history data is supported by citation to Millar, 1989.

claim: Juveniles of P. maniculatus first leave the nest between 14 and 16 days of age.
source: Juveniles first leave the nest between 14 and 16 days of age (Vestal et al., 1980) and become independent of their mother between 18 and 25 days (Millar, 1989).
evidence: This developmental timing is supported by citation to Vestal et al., 1980.

claim: P. maniculatus juveniles become independent of their mother between 18 and 25 days.
source: Juveniles first leave the nest between 14 and 16 days of age (Vestal et al., 1980) and become independent of their mother between 18 and 25 days (Millar, 1989).
evidence: This developmental timing is supported by citation to Millar, 1989.

claim: Captive P. maniculatus females give birth to their first litter, on average, at 84 days.
source: Captive females give birth to their first litter, on average, at 84 days (Haigh, 1983), but males are capable of siring offspring several weeks earlier.
evidence: This reproductive timing is supported by citation to Haigh, 1983.

claim: Male P. maniculatus are capable of siring offspring several weeks earlier than females give birth to their first litter.
source: Captive females give birth to their first litter, on average, at 84 days (Haigh, 1983), but males are capable of siring offspring several weeks earlier.
evidence: This sex difference in reproductive timing is stated directly.

claim: In response to short day length, many Peromyscus species exhibit seasonal gonadal regression.
source: In response to short day length, many species exhibit seasonal gonadal regression (Trainor et al., 2006), increased aggression (Trainor et al., 2007), impaired spatial memory (Workman et al., 2009) and enhanced immune function (Prendergast and Nelson, 2001).
evidence: This photoperiodic response is supported by citation to Trainor et al., 2006.

claim: In response to short day length, many Peromyscus species exhibit increased aggression.
source: In response to short day length, many species exhibit seasonal gonadal regression (Trainor et al., 2006), increased aggression (Trainor et al., 2007), impaired spatial memory (Workman et al., 2009) and enhanced immune function (Prendergast and Nelson, 2001).
evidence: This photoperiodic response is supported by citation to Trainor et al., 2007.

claim: In response to short day length, many Peromyscus species exhibit impaired spatial memory.
source: In response to short day length, many species exhibit seasonal gonadal regression (Trainor et al., 2006), increased aggression (Trainor et al., 2007), impaired spatial memory (Workman et al., 2009) and enhanced immune function (Prendergast and Nelson, 2001).
evidence: This photoperiodic response is supported by citation to Workman et al., 2009.

claim: In response to short day length, many Peromyscus species exhibit enhanced immune function.
source: In response to short day length, many species exhibit seasonal gonadal regression (Trainor et al., 2006), increased aggression (Trainor et al., 2007), impaired spatial memory (Workman et al., 2009) and enhanced immune function (Prendergast and Nelson, 2001).
evidence: This photoperiodic response is supported by citation to Prendergast and Nelson, 2001.

claim: Day length can reverse the behavioral action of the hormone estradiol by determining which estrogen receptor pathway is expressed and consequently activated.
source: For example, day length can reverse the behavioral action of the hormone estradiol by determining which estrogen receptor pathway is expressed and consequently activated (Trainor et al., 2007).
evidence: This mechanistic finding is supported by citation to Trainor et al., 2007.

claim: Substantial genetic variation exists in the neuroendocrine pathways that control reproductive timing in Peromyscus.
source: While life history traits are strongly affected by environmental cues, substantial genetic variation in the neuroendocrine pathways that control reproductive timing also exists, as demonstrated by selection line experiments with photoperiod responsive and nonresponsive P. leucopus (Heideman et al., 1999; Heideman and Pittman, 2009).
evidence: This genetic variation is demonstrated by selection experiments cited to Heideman et al., 1999 and Heideman and Pittman, 2009.

claim: The majority of Peromyscus species are promiscuous.
source: While the majority of Peromyscus species are promiscuous, monogamy has independently evolved at least twice in the genus (Turner et al., 2010).
evidence: This mating system characterization is stated and supported by citation to Turner et al., 2010.

claim: Monogamy has independently evolved at least twice in the genus Peromyscus.
source: While the majority of Peromyscus species are promiscuous, monogamy has independently evolved at least twice in the genus (Turner et al., 2010).
evidence: This evolutionary pattern is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2010.

claim: Peromyscus californicus is socially and genetically monogamous.
source: Both Peromyscus californicus (Gubernick and Alberts, 1987; Ribble, 1991) and Peromyscus polionotus (Smith, 1966; Foltz, 1981) are socially and genetically monogamous, and both males and females contribute to the care of offspring.
evidence: This mating system characterization is supported by citations to Gubernick and Alberts, 1987 and Ribble, 1991.

claim: Peromyscus polionotus is socially and genetically monogamous.
source: Both Peromyscus californicus (Gubernick and Alberts, 1987; Ribble, 1991) and Peromyscus polionotus (Smith, 1966; Foltz, 1981) are socially and genetically monogamous, and both males and females contribute to the care of offspring.
evidence: This mating system characterization is supported by citations to Smith, 1966 and Foltz, 1981.

claim: In P. californicus and P. polionotus, both males and females contribute to the care of offspring.
source: Both Peromyscus californicus (Gubernick and Alberts, 1987; Ribble, 1991) and Peromyscus polionotus (Smith, 1966; Foltz, 1981) are socially and genetically monogamous, and both males and females contribute to the care of offspring.
evidence: This parental care pattern is stated directly in the context of monogamous species.

claim: P. californicus has become an important neurobiological model for the study of male parental care.
source: P. californicus, in particular, has become an important neurobiological model for the study of male parental care (Bester-Meredith et al., 1999; Trainor et al., 2003; Lee and Brown, 2007; de Jong et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: This model system status is supported by multiple citations documenting neurobiological studies.

claim: Monogamous P. polionotus can hybridize with promiscuous P. maniculatus.
source: As a complement, the ability of monogamous P. polionotus to hybridize with promiscuous P. maniculatus allows geneticists to identify the genetic basis of alternate mating systems and their associated phenotypes, from genomic imprinting (Vrana et al., 2000) to parental investment and reproductive traits (e.g., Fisher and Hoekstra, 2010).
evidence: This hybridization capability is stated directly and supported by citations to studies using this approach.

claim: Parental and social behaviors are particularly vulnerable to endocrine disruption.
source: Rosenfeld (2015) argues that parental and social behaviors are particularly vulnerable to endocrine disruption, as these traits are dependent upon the organizational and activational effects of androgens and estrogens.
evidence: This argument is attributed to and supported by citation to Rosenfeld, 2015.

claim: P. maniculatus males exposed to BPA during development displayed reduced spatial learning and exploratory behavior.
source: P. maniculatus males exposed to the endocrine disrupting compound bisphenol A (BPA) during development displayed reduced spatial learning and exploratory behavior—traits known to be associated with male–male competition for mates (Galea et al., 1996; Jašarević et al., 2011).
evidence: This experimental finding is supported by citations to Galea et al., 1996 and Jašarević et al., 2011.

claim: Spatial learning and exploratory behavior are traits associated with male-male competition for mates.
source: P. maniculatus males exposed to the endocrine disrupting compound bisphenol A (BPA) during development displayed reduced spatial learning and exploratory behavior—traits known to be associated with male–male competition for mates (Galea et al., 1996; Jašarević et al., 2011).
evidence: This behavioral association is supported by citations to Galea et al., 1996 and Jašarević et al., 2011.

claim: Spatial learning and exploratory behavior were unaffected in BPA-exposed female P. maniculatus.
source: However, these behaviors—which are not subject to sexual selection in females—were unaffected in BPA-exposed females.
evidence: This sex-specific finding is stated directly in contrast to the male results.

claim: Mate guarding and territorial behavior in monogamous P. californicus males are compromised by endocrine disruption.
source: By contrast, sexual selection favors the evolution of mate guarding and territorial behavior in monogamous males, and it is these traits (rather than spatial learning or exploratory behavior) that are compromised by endocrine disruption in P. californicus (Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to Williams et al., 2013.

claim: P. maniculatus digs short, simple burrows.
source: For instance, P. maniculatus and P. polionotus display considerable differences in stereotyped burrowing behavior. P. maniculatus digs short, simple burrows in contrast to the long, complex burrows constructed by P. polionotus that consist of an entrance tunnel, nest chamber and escape tunnel (Dawson et al., 1988; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This behavioral description is supported by citations to Dawson et al., 1988 and Weber et al., 2013.

claim: P. polionotus constructs long, complex burrows that consist of an entrance tunnel, nest chamber and escape tunnel.
source: For instance, P. maniculatus and P. polionotus display considerable differences in stereotyped burrowing behavior. P. maniculatus digs short, simple burrows in contrast to the long, complex burrows constructed by P. polionotus that consist of an entrance tunnel, nest chamber and escape tunnel (Dawson et al., 1988; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This behavioral description is supported by citations to Dawson et al., 1988 and Weber et al., 2013.

claim: Mice raised in the laboratory for several generations recapitulate the species-specific burrow architectures observed in nature.
source: Remarkably, mice raised in the laboratory for several generations recapitulate the species-specific burrow architectures observed in nature (Video 1).
evidence: This finding is stated directly and illustrated in Video 1.

claim: The complex burrows of P. polionotus are derived.
